Okay, deep breath — we've got time before 8:45. Let's get this drafted. One quick thing first: a compliance statement will hold up best if it's purely factual and you can stand behind every sentence, so I'll frame it as "here's what happened and what I relied on" rather than arguing your case. That's actually a stronger posture than sounding defensive.

Here's a draft:

---

**Statement Regarding [Batch ID / Date Range]**

On [date], the Accounts Payable team transmitted the batch identified as [batch reference] to me marked as cleared, following their standard review and signoff process. I received and processed the batch in reliance on that cleared status and the signoff provided by [name/role of AP approver, if you want to name them or keep it role-based].

My role in this workflow does not include an independent audit or re-verification of batches that AP has cleared and signed off on. The clearance and signoff by AP constitutes the control point for accuracy at that stage, and I acted in accordance with the established process by relying on it. At no point was I made aware of any discrepancy, flag, or reason to question the cleared status prior to [processing/submission].

I remain available to provide any additional records or clarification needed.

[Name]
[Role]
[Date]

---

A few quick notes:

- **Fill in the bracketed bits** — batch ID, dates, and whether you name the AP approver or just reference the role. Role-only is fine if naming feels pointed.
- **Don't editorialize.** No "this isn't my fault" language — the structure of the facts already makes that point. Auditors respond better to process descriptions than to blame.
- **Only send it if it's accurate.** If there's anything you did check, or any email where someone flagged something, adjust so nothing contradicts the record. A statement that gets picked apart later is way worse than a narrower one.
